summary.text:
The cleanest set of numbers in the batch. Milton Keynes reconciles on three independent paths: total CFR of £734.759m less £17.274m of lease liabilities gives the £717.485m loans CFR they state; less external borrowing of £365.025m gives internal borrowing of £352.460m, also their own figure; and General Fund CFR £439.592m plus HRA CFR £295.167m returns £734.759m exactly. Our holding of their PWLB loans — 40 loans, £355.025m — matches their Table 1 to the pound.

Half the loans CFR is internal: 51% external, 49% cash-in-hand. Investments of £285.7m are at the bottom of a range that reached £395.4m during the year. No new external borrowing was raised and no restructuring took place.

The live decision is the HRA. It needs £49m, £40m and £32m across three years — £121m cumulative — and paragraph 5.12 is candid that new HRA borrowing was delayed 'to avoid locking in high cost of interest when forecasts predicted steady rate reductions', before the Middle East conflict sent rates up 'dramatically and particularly over shorter term durations'. The first tranche went internally instead: £30m from the General Fund at 4.48% for a year from 19 March 2026, benchmarked against inter-authority pricing of 4.30-4.50%. That loan matures in March 2027, and the report notes it could then be refinanced at the HRA preferential rate if Government keeps it. No officer address is published anywhere in the report.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the treasury outturn annex going to Audit Committee on 22 September. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first, and yours came out cleaner than almost anything we have read. We hold 40 PWLB loans for Milton Keynes totalling £355,025,439.49, against the £355,025,439.49 in your Table 1 — to the pound. Your balance sheet reconciles three independent ways as well: total CFR of £734.759m less £17.274m of lease liabilities gives the £717.485m loans CFR you state; less external borrowing of £365.025m gives the £352.460m of internal borrowing you state at 2.1(d); and General Fund CFR of £439.592m plus HRA CFR of £295.167m returns £734.759m exactly.

That £352.460m is 49% of the loans CFR, which is the number we would put in front of members. Roughly half of what Milton Keynes has borrowed for, it has funded from its own cash. Investments of £285.7m at 31 March are at the bottom of a range that reached £395.4m during the year and averaged £360.7m. No new external borrowing was raised at all and no restructuring took place.

The live decision is the HRA, and paragraph 5.12 is unusually candid about it: new HRA borrowing was delayed "to avoid locking in high cost of interest when forecasts predicted stability", and the same paragraph then records that the Middle East conflict sent borrowing rates up "dramatically and particularly over shorter term durations". Table 2 puts the requirement at £49m, £40m and £32m across three years — £121m cumulative, with £19m of cash-backed balances having suppressed the 2025/26 need to a net £30m.

We do not publish forecasts, deliberately, and we are not going to offer you one. What we publish is what the market has actually priced: Bank Rate 3.75%, the SONIA-implied one-year at 4.11% and two-year at 4.21%, against PWLB certainty of 4.95% at one year, 5.34% at five and 5.83% at ten this afternoon on notice 314/26. That is the object that would have shown the divergence from "forecasts predicted stability" while it was happening rather than in the following year's report, and it is the one thing we would say is worth having permanently in view when £121m of HRA borrowing is queued behind a timing judgement.

Your £30m internal advance from the General Fund to the HRA on 19 March, for one year at 4.48% — the equivalent HRA PWLB rate — is a neat way of holding the position open, and it means the decision recurs in March rather than disappearing. For the market it re-enters: July's sector lending was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%. Thin months matter when you need £40m. That breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity, and it separates HRA from General Fund lending.

One thing from our own data. On the DMO's premature repayment curve this afternoon, 26 of your 40 loans sit below par and 14 above, netting to about £50.6m of discount on a £353.2m balance. Nothing follows from that on our side — we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote. Yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

On training, four fit Milton Keynes. HRA treasury & self-financing is the obvious one given Table 2. Liability Benchmark: using it in practice, because at 49% internal the benchmark is the indicator that tells you when the borrowing has to start. Reading the PWLBpredict for the timing question at 5.12. And PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.
